Capacitor. A two-terminal passive component that stores electrical energy in an electric field between two conducting plates separated by an insulating material called a dielectric. Capacitance is measured in farads, though practical values are typically in microfarads or nanofarads.

Capacitance itself is defined as the ratio of charge stored to applied voltage. The dielectric material—ceramic, film, or electrolytic—determines the breakdown voltage and capacitance density; a higher permittivity allows for a smaller physical size. Electrolytic capacitors are polarized and marked with positive and negative terminals. Exceeding the reverse voltage destroys the dielectric and causes catastrophic failure.

In steady direct current, a capacitor acts as an open circuit. But in alternating current or during charging and discharging, it passes current. The RC time constant, calculated as resistance times capacitance in seconds, governs how quickly the capacitor charges and discharges. At one time constant, the capacitor voltage reaches roughly sixty-three percent of the applied voltage.

When capacitors are arranged in series, they follow a reciprocal rule: one over the total capacitance equals one over the first capacitance plus one over the second. In parallel, they simply add together. Capacitors block direct current, which is why they are used in AC coupling, but they pass alternating current through, making them essential for filtering high-frequency noise. Coupling capacitors decouple AC signals between stages, while bypass capacitors shunt high-frequency noise to ground near supply pins.
